extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy, reformers and policymakers interested in land reform and theories of property
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length argumentative treatment of whether private property in land can be justified and whether landowners should be compensated if land is resumed by the community; combines moral, legal, historical, and economic reasoning against compensation and private landownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral illegitimacy of exclusive land ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: There is and can be no just title to an exclusive possession of the soil; private property in land is a 'bold, bare, enormous wrong,' comparable to chattel slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument elaborates that land appropriation is a continuous robbery — levying rent on present production and depriving present and future persons of their birthright. The text insists that justice requires abolition of exclusive private land ownership rather than accommodation or compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between land and produced goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Property in land differs essentially from property in things of human production and has no warrant in abstract justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter urges readers not to conflate land with goods produced by labor. Standard economic treatments tacitly admit the difference, but public habit and legal custom obscure it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of justice and expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: Abolishing private property in land is both just and expedient because private ownership is the primary cause of poverty, misery, degradation, social disease, and political weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses empirical and moral claims: since land appropriation harms general welfare, both moral right and practical benefit demand abolition; remedies that preserve landholders’ interests will fail to cure underlying social ills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of compensation on moral grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: If the land belongs to the people, it is absurd in morality and justice that the people should pay its salable value to proprietors upon resumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that compensating proprietors would be paying people for what already belongs to the community; it would be unjust to transfer public wealth to private holders in the name of compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal precedent about innocent purchasers (no automatic compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under common law, an innocent possessor whose title is found defective has no claim to compensation; law often allows the rightful owner to be put in possession and may take improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an analogy: if courts do not compensate innocent buyers of wrongfully-held land, public resumption need not compensate landholders; law sometimes requires surrender of improvements and accounting of profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical objection to state purchase at market price
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchasing individual proprietorship at market prices would be cumbrous, extend government functions, breed corruption, and economically saddle producers with payment of speculative rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: market price includes expectation of future increases; the state would pay interest on purchase money while also effectively collecting rents — making the state an agent of landholders and imposing heavier burdens on labor and capital in the interim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation perpetuates unjust advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Buying up land at market rates would preserve the unjust advantage of landholders in another form and continue the unjust disadvantage of non-landholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if future gains eventually exceed purchase interest, compensation leaves a class in possession of enormous advantage; purchase thus fails to remedy the fundamental wrong and may delay relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Mill’s limited resumption plan
rubrics_metrics.description: John Stuart Mill’s proposal to appropriate only the future unearned increase in land value is inadequate because it leaves a class permanently in possession of a large advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter explains that Mill’s fixation of present market value and appropriation of future increments would not eliminate the existing injustice and would preserve substantial privileges of landholders; it might be 'better than nothing' but is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic claim: rent is community-created and thus belongs to the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Rent does not arise spontaneously from land nor from proprietor effort; it is a value created by the whole community and therefore rightfully belongs to the whole community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports reappropriation without compensating proprietors because the community generates land value; allowing private capture of rent is theft from collective creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical argument: common right to land is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, the common right to land was the primary and persistent perception; private ownership arose via usurpation (war, conquest, sacerdotal/legal manipulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter surveys cross-cultural evidence that primitive societies treated land as communal; private property in land is presented as an artificial, later development, weakening the case for moral claims by modern proprietors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feudal tenure implies conditional/collective ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Feudalism, while recognizing individual enjoyment of land, treated it as a trust subordinate to the sovereign/collective; tenure included obligations and limited alienability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show that even systems commonly thought to affirm absolute private ownership historically imposed duties and acknowledged a superior collective right — undermining claims to absolute, compensable title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible minimal protection for holders upon resumption
rubrics_metrics.description: People resuming ownership need not confiscate all personal property or improvements; landholders may retain improvements and personal property to avoid oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author states he does not advocate taking improvements from honest possessor; practical resumption can allow owners to keep improvements while reasserting communal land ownership — a policy choice to reduce hardship while remedying structural injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of compensation as pragmatic excuse rooted in habit and ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: The reluctance to abolish private land ownership and the insistence on compensating proprietors stem from mental habits, deference to 'vested rights', and acceptance of Malthusian ideas about scarcity and wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter frames compensation demands as ideological obstacles rather than principled necessities; overcoming habitual reverence for property is part of political change.
